title: How to Test Your Hotel Website on Mobile in 30 Minutes
excerpt: A simple do-it-yourself mobile test for hotel and homestay websites: who to test with, tasks to give, what to watch for, a findings table and how to fix problems in priority order.
description: A 30-minute DIY mobile user test for hotel websites: 3-5 testers, real booking tasks, what to watch for, a findings table and fixes in priority order.
html:
You can test your hotel website on mobile in about 30 minutes with three to five people who are not on your team. Give each person a phone and a few real tasks, such as finding room prices, checking policies, starting a booking and contacting you on WhatsApp. Watch silently, note where they hesitate, then fix the biggest problems first.

Why a small DIY test is worth doing

Owners and managers know their own website too well to see its problems. You know where the cancellation policy is hidden and which menu item leads to rates. A guest arriving from Google or Instagram on a phone does not. Watching a handful of real people try to use the site shows you, very quickly, the places where guests get stuck, give up and go back to MakeMyTrip or Booking.com.

A small test will not give you statistics, and it does not need to. Usability practitioners commonly work with small groups because the same serious problems tend to appear with the first few people. Your aim is to find those problems, not to measure them.

Who to test with

Pick three to five people who roughly resemble your guests and have not worked on the website:

  • Friends or relatives who travel the way your guests do (families, couples, groups).
  • Recent guests willing to help, perhaps with a small thank-you such as a meal voucher.
  • Someone less comfortable with technology, if some of your guests are older.

Avoid your web developer, your staff and anyone who has seen the site often. Ask each person to use their own phone if possible, because that is how guests will see it, including their screen size, browser and data connection.

Prepare the test in ten minutes

  • Write down five or six tasks on a sheet (below).
  • Decide on a realistic scenario: "You are planning a two-night trip for two adults next month."
  • Open a blank findings table to fill in as you watch.
  • If the person is remote, use a video call where they share their phone screen.
  • Tell them: "We are testing the website, not you. There are no wrong answers. Please think out loud as you go."

Tasks to give testers

Give tasks one at a time, in plain words, without using the labels on your website. If your menu says "Accommodation", do not say "find the accommodation page"; say "find out what rooms they have".

  1. Find the price: "Find out how much a room for two would cost for a Friday and Saturday next month."
  2. Check a policy: "Find out what happens if you need to cancel a week before."
  3. Check a practical detail: "Find out whether breakfast is included and whether there is parking." Swap in what guests most often ask you, such as pets, check-in time or distance to the beach.
  4. Start a booking: "Go as far as you can to book that room, but stop before paying."
  5. Contact the property: "Send them a message on WhatsApp asking if an early check-in is possible."
  6. Find the location: "Find out how you would get there from the nearest railway station or airport."

Give each task a few minutes. If someone is completely stuck, note it and move on.

What to watch for

Stay quiet. The hardest part is not helping. When a tester hesitates, that hesitation is the finding. Look out for:

  • Hesitation: long pauses before tapping, scrolling up and down looking for something.
  • Wrong turns: tapping a menu item that does not lead where they expected.
  • Tap problems: buttons too small, links too close together, things that look tappable but are not.
  • Pop-ups and overlays: chat widgets, offers or cookie banners covering the content or the booking button.
  • Slow loading: waiting for galleries or the booking engine; comments like "is it loading?"
  • Surprises: a price that changes when taxes are added, a booking engine that opens in a new window with a different design, a WhatsApp link that does not open the app.
  • Things they say: "I would just call", "I would check on MakeMyTrip", "where is the price?"

Record findings in a simple table

Fill this in during or just after each session. Keep observations factual: what happened, not what you think caused it.

TaskWhat happenedTesters affectedSeverityPossible fix
Find the priceLooked for prices on room pages; only found them after opening the booking engine4 of 5HighShow "from" rates on room pages and a "check availability" button
Check cancellation policyCould not find it; one found it in the footer3 of 5HighLink the policy from room pages and the booking step
WhatsApp contactChat widget covered the WhatsApp button2 of 5MediumRemove one of the two, keep WhatsApp
Find locationMap loaded slowly; no written directions2 of 5MediumAdd written directions from station and airport

The rows above are an illustrative example of how to fill the table, not real results.

Fix in priority order

Rank each problem by two questions: does it stop people booking or contacting you, and how many testers hit it? Then work in this order:

  1. Blockers: anything that stopped someone finding the price, booking or contacting you.
  2. Trust problems: hidden policies, unclear totals, broken links, outdated information.
  3. Friction: slow pages, small buttons, confusing menu labels, pop-ups.
  4. Polish: wording, layout and visual issues that annoyed but did not stop anyone.

Many top fixes are quick: moving the WhatsApp button, adding "from" prices, linking the cancellation policy. Others, like a slow booking engine, need your developer or booking engine provider. For speed specifically, see our guide to mobile SEO and page speed for hotel websites. For problems inside the booking flow itself, see our post on booking engine conversion.

Test again after changes

Once you have fixed the top problems, run the same tasks with two or three new people. You will usually find that the old blockers are gone and a new, smaller set of issues appears. Repeat the test whenever you redesign a page, change your booking engine or add a new feature such as online payment by UPI. Our conversion optimisation page explains how testing fits into a longer programme of improvements.

Frequently asked questions

Is testing with only five people enough?

For finding major problems, a small group is usually enough, because the most serious issues tend to show up repeatedly with the first few testers. You are looking for obstacles, not statistics. Running several small rounds, fixing problems in between, is generally more useful than one large test.

Should I test on my phone or theirs?

Theirs, wherever possible. Testers' own phones reflect real screen sizes, browsers, settings and data connections, including slower ones. If you must lend a phone, choose an ordinary mid-range Android phone rather than a high-end device, since many of your guests will be using something similar.

What if testers just say the website looks nice?

Opinions about looks are not what you are testing. Focus on what they do, not what they say. Did they find the price, the policy and the WhatsApp button, and how long did it take? Asking them to think out loud during tasks gives more useful information than asking for opinions afterwards.

Can I test the booking engine if it is run by another company?

Yes. Ask testers to go as far as the payment step and stop. Problems you find, such as a slow load, a confusing date picker or a price that changes at checkout, can be shared with your booking engine provider. Some can be fixed in its settings; others may be a reason to compare providers.

Where to start

Write the six tasks above on a sheet, adjusting the practical-detail task to your guests' most common question. Book three people for 30 minutes each this week, watch them use their own phones, and fill in the findings table. Fix the top two blockers before testing again.
